problemText: Benjamin Franklin's 1754 cartoon shows a snake cut into eight segments labeled by colony, captioned "JOIN, or DIE," drawing on the folk belief that a severed snake could recover if rejoined before sunset. Originally published during the French and Indian War, this image was revived as a political symbol in the 1760s and 1770s primarily because it —
choices: warned colonists that reconciliation with Britain was still the surest path to lasting economic prosperity
proved the colonies had already formed a permanent political union under the Continental Congress
captured the call for colonial unity, now against imperial taxation not France
mocked Parliament's repeated failure to pass effective legislation regulating colonial trade
hints: Ask what threat the colonies faced in the 1760s-1770s, compared to the threat they faced in 1754.
The cartoon's core message is about unity in the face of a common danger — only the danger changed.

problemText: In Common Sense (January 1776), Thomas Paine writes, "Freedom hath been hunted round the globe... O! receive the fugitive, and prepare in time an asylum for mankind." This appeal reflects which development in the imperial crisis leading to independence?
choices: Growing colonial conviction that America's cause was universal, no longer mere loyalty to Britain
Widespread colonial enthusiasm for restoring the exact pre-1763 terms of the imperial relationship with Britain
The colonies' formal declaration of war against France following the close of the Seven Years' War
Colonial support for keeping the monarchy but replacing George III with a more sympathetic ruler
hints: Paine published this pamphlet months after Lexington and Concord, when many colonists still hoped for reconciliation.
Notice that Paine frames American liberty as a refuge for 'mankind,' not just for British subjects.

problemText: The Declaration of Independence states that governments are "instituted among Men, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed." This claim draws most directly on which Enlightenment idea?
choices: Mercantilist theory that colonies exist mainly to enrich the mother country through controlled trade
Thomas Hobbes's argument that only an all-powerful sovereign can prevent a state of perpetual war
The doctrine of the divine right of kings, holding that monarchs answer to God alone
John Locke's social-contract theory that legitimate authority rests on the consent of the governed
hints: Ask where political power comes from in this sentence — from a monarch, or from the people themselves?
This is the same philosopher whose ideas about natural rights (life, liberty, property) shaped the Declaration's opening.

problemText: Patrick Henry declares, "give me liberty, or give me death!" while the Declaration of Independence asserts that among unalienable rights are "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness." Both statements most directly reflect which shared revolutionary-era idea?
choices: That political authority should rest exclusively with a hereditary aristocracy
That liberty is a natural right worth risking life itself to secure
That economic self-sufficiency mattered more to the colonists than political rights
That the colonies should remain part of the British Empire under a reformed constitution
hints: Both speakers set liberty against the alternative of death or the loss of self-government.
Think about what makes liberty a 'natural right' rather than a privilege granted by a king.

problemText: The Preamble to the Constitution states its purpose is "to form a more perfect Union" and "provide for the common defence." This phrasing most directly reflects criticism of which prior arrangement?
choices: The Articles of Confederation, whose weak Congress could neither tax states nor fund defense
The British colonial administration that governed the colonies before the imperial crisis of 1763
The system of appointed royal governors who separately administered each individual colony under the crown
The Continental Army's wartime command structure during the years of the Revolutionary War
hints: 'More perfect Union' implies improving upon an existing union — which national government existed right before the Constitution?
Recall that the Confederation Congress could not levy taxes or compel states to fund a national defense.

problemText: The Declaration of Independence's preamble asserts that governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed." Drawing on this principle and the colonists' broader revolutionary-era distrust of concentrated power, the framers of the Articles of Confederation (1781) most directly chose to —
choices: create a strong single national executive modeled closely on the powers of the British monarchy
establish a permanent national army answerable directly to Congress rather than to the individual states
design a national government with no independent executive, leaving most authority to the states
abolish the state governments entirely in favor of one single unified national government
hints: Think about what the revolutionaries were most afraid of repeating, given what they had just declared independence from.
The Articles created a Congress with no president and no power to tax — a deliberate reaction, not an oversight.

problemText: In Federalist No. 10 (1787), James Madison defines a faction as "a number of citizens... united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to... the permanent and aggregate interests of the community." Madison's point of view in this definition is best described as —
choices: an Anti-Federalist's fear that a powerful national government would itself become the worst tyrannical faction
a British loyalist's argument that the colonial assemblies were incapable of genuine self-government
a Democratic-Republican's defense of states' rights against federal encroachment by the national government
a Federalist's concern that unchecked factions could threaten minority rights and the common good
hints: Madison wrote the Federalist essays to persuade states to ratify the Constitution he had helped draft.
Ask whose interests Madison worries a faction might trample — and why he thinks the new Constitution's structure could help.

problemText: Brutus No. 1 (1787) warns, "History furnishes no example of a free republic, any thing like the extent of the United States," pointing to the fall of the Grecian and Roman republics after they "extended their conquests over large territories." Compared to Madison's argument in Federalist No. 10 that a large republic best controls the dangers of faction, Brutus's argument most directly —
choices: agrees that a large territory strengthens republican government by diluting the influence of any single faction
reaches the opposite conclusion: a free republic cannot survive over so vast a territory
focuses on the same issue of factions but concludes that only a monarchy can control them
ignores the size of the republic entirely, focusing instead on the question of representation in the Senate
hints: Madison says size is the cure for faction; ask what Brutus says size does to a republic's survival.
Brutus is an Anti-Federalist essay opposing ratification — expect it to contradict a core Federalist argument.

problemText: The Preamble to the Constitution pledges that the new government would "insure domestic Tranquility" and "promote the general Welfare." Which development in the 1790s most directly tested this pledge?
choices: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803, which peacefully doubled the territorial size of the United States
The ratification of the Bill of Rights, which added explicit protections for individual liberties
The Whiskey Rebellion, in which Pennsylvania farmers violently resisted a new federal excise tax
The Marbury v. Madison decision, which first established the principle of judicial review
hints: Look for an event in the 1790s (not the 1800s) that directly challenged whether the new government could keep 'domestic Tranquility.'
This event tested whether the federal government could enforce its own tax laws against armed resistance.

problemText: In Federalist No. 10, Madison defines a faction as a group "united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adverse to... the permanent and aggregate interests of the community," and argues the Constitution's structure would control such factions. Which development in the new republic of the 1790s complicates Madison's confidence?
choices: The peaceful transfer of power from Washington to Adams in 1797, proving Madison's structure worked exactly as intended
The Whiskey Rebellion, which showed that factions posed no real threat to the new government
The Alien and Sedition Acts, which eliminated political disagreement entirely within the new republic
The emergence of the Federalist and Democratic-Republican parties, durable factions the Constitution was meant to prevent
hints: Think about what formed around Hamilton's and Jefferson's rival visions during Washington's administration.
Madison hoped the Constitution's structure would prevent durable national factions — did it succeed by the late 1790s?
